Question: How can scientists create measuring tools more accurate than the tools we already have? Doesn't the accuracy of new tools depend on the accuracy of the tools used to make it?

text:
Hi Sam,

Good question, and honestly a bit of a mystery until you see it up close. That little ball (or in some whistles a piece of charcoal or a pellet you can feel rattling around) sits inside a sealed chamber that the air from your lips is pushed into. Your breath forms a tight jet and the ball gets caught in the turbulence of it, so it bounces around the chamber instead of just sitting still.

Every time the ball smacks into the walls of that little room, it sets the air inside vibrating, and the shape and size of the chamber decides what pitch you get out of that vibration. So the ball is basically the thing that converts your steady stream of breath into the actual noise. Take it out and the same amount of air just hisses through; you might get a faint whistle from the jet impinging on a sharp edge, but it's weak and unreliable, exactly like a jet engine without the fan.

In the old pea-whistle design the "pea" is what gives it that slightly gritty, rattly tone, and because it moves around it also means the note isn't super consistent - you get a wobbly pitch that's really useful for a referee (hard to tune a protest to) but annoying if you're trying to match a song. Sports whistles mostly use a fixed plastic redirector instead of a free ball now because it gives a cleaner, louder, more consistent note, but the principle is the same: something has to knock on the air in that chamber to make it sing.

Hope that makes sense - next time you have one, take the cap off and crack it open, you can see it.

Cheers,
Alex

text:
Hey Sam,

Good question, and one of those things you see a hundred times without really thinking about it. That little ball (or disc, on some whistles) sitting in the middle of the mouthpiece is called the fipple, or sometimes the "whistle plug" or "rider."

Here is what it actually does. When you blow into a whistle, the air hits that ball at an angle and gets split: part of it is deflected sharply across a thin edge (the "lipping" or fipple edge), and that sudden deflection creates a jet of air that vibrates back and forth really fast. That vibration is what you hear as the note. Without the ball, the air would just blow straight through the hole like a whoosh and you would get no pitch at all, just a puff of wind.

So the ball is basically forcing the air stream into a narrow jet at the right angle and speed to make it oscillate. The size and shape of the channel around it, plus the length of the tube behind it, set what note you get. That is why a big referee whistle sounds lower and a tiny toy whistle sounds so shrill.

On a pea whistle (the classic referee kind) there is also a little ball that rattles around inside the tube. That one is a different thing entirely: when you blow, it bounces around and interrupts the air stream in a chaotic way, which is what gives it that loud, buzzy "pea bobble" sound instead of a clean note. Coaches love those because the rattle is so hard to miss over a crowd.

Hope that explains it. Let me know if you want me to draw you a little diagram of the air path, because honestly that is easier to see than to read about.

Cheers,
Alex

text:
Hi Maria,

Great question, I was actually curious about this myself. There are a few reasons it makes more sense than you'd think.

First, the Catholics. Morrissey was famously, almost aggressively Catholic growing up, and his early lyrics are full of confession, guilt, saints, and longing in a very religious way. That resonates a lot with Catholic Latino listeners in a way that, say, Iggy Pop never did. All that stuff about pity and suffering is basically penance set to music.

Second, timing. He came up in the early eighties, exactly when a bunch of Latino kids in the Bronx, East LA, and Houston were discovering rock through radio and older cousins' record collections. When you're sixteen and someone's screaming into a microphone about being heartbroken and surrounded by gypsies, it just hits. Heartbreak doesn't care what language you speak.

Third, once a few older Latinos liked him, it became a family thing. You hear "The More I See You" at your tita's house on a Wednesday afternoon and now you're a fan forever, no choice in the matter.

Anyway, that's my best answer.

Love,
Dave

text:
Hi Sam,

Good question. I think it's mostly that they proved out. A lot of fads leave nothing behind, but the Beatles kept writing their own songs, and those songs turned out to be genuinely good stuff that people still play fifty years later. "Yesterday" and " HELP!" don't age like pop fodder.

Second, they were ahead of the curve on so much: the studio as an instrument, on-record layers, the debut of the album as an actual piece of art with Revolver and Sgt. Pepper's, the concert-to-studio thing on Abbey Road. Producers and musicians kept learning from them for decades. A fad doesn't have a legacy like that sitting in a master tape library.

And there's survivorship: the other boy bands of 1964, the Hollyberries and the like, just vanished, which makes the Beatles look like the one that was real all along. Plus Beatlesmania's awkwardness got romanticized later. It's easier to write a hagiography about screaming girls than about, say, a trio of guy singers from Leeds.

So: songs that held up + influence that compounded + everyone else evaporating.

Let me know if you want album recs.

Cheers
Alex

text:
Hey Sam,

Great question, I've been thinking about this a lot lately.

Honestly there are a few things that line up, and they tend to reinforce each other.

First, what's actually moddable depends on how the game was built. If the game ships with accessible data files - textures, maps, item definitions, that kind of thing - people can start tweaking within an hour, no programming needed. Minecraft and Terraria basically hand you the keys. Skyrim's case is a bit different: the game itself isn't super friendly, but it runs on the Creation Engine, and Bethesda kept releasing new games on that engine (Oblivion, FO3, New Vegas), so a whole pile of people already knew the engine and tools like ScriptExtender. A huge chunk of a modding community is just "is it easy to make your first tiny change?"

Second, the game needs to be a template, not a product. Games like Minecraft and Skyrim are really blank-ish: open world, no guided story, tons of space for you to put stuff. Mods extend that in directions the developers couldn't have predicted - new biomes, new quests, adding dragons, whatever. A game that's a tightly designed two-hour experience doesn't really have seams for you to stick stuff into. A mod that adds a story to a game with a story usually fights the original story, so people get frustrated and stop.

Third, the developer's attitude matters more than people think. When a publisher actively supports mods - provides an editor, hosts a workshop, lets you sell what you make (Skyrim's Workshop and Steam Workshop, or FFXIV being mod-friendly in a narrow way) - the community explodes. When a company treats mods as potential piracy ("just buy my game 2") or the engine is locked down and embarrassing to work with, nothing takes off. Kingdoms of Amalur is a fun example of this: decent game, locked-down engine, dev basically ignored modding, mod scene is basically nothing.

Fourth, timing and luck: if a game hits at a moment when its player base overlaps with an existing modding ecosystem, it inherits people. Skyrim launching right after a big Bethesda modding scene already existed helped a ton.

So the short version: readable files or a real editor, a game design that leaves room to add stuff, and devs who don't actively fight you. Miss two of those three and you get zero mod scene, no matter how good the game is.

Anyway, let me know if you want recommendations - I found some mods for that space game you like.

- Alex

text:
Hey Alex,

Great question — I finally have an answer for you! It turns out pandas' clumsy reputation is mostly a diet thing. They eat almost nothing but bamboo, which is a lousy energy source, so they burn way fewer calories than other bears and just can't afford to be active. They loaf around a lot instead of hunting or exploring, so their motor skills got pretty little evolutionary pressure to stay sharp.

There are also some physical quirks. Their "thumb" isn't even a real thumb — it's a modified wrist bone that they use to grip bamboo stalks. It's fine for peeling stems, but it doesn't make for a very sure hand for climbing or dexterity in general. That, plus their stocky build and small heads, makes them look especially wobbly on camera.

They're actually not that bad at climbing when they're young cubs, and they swim fine. It's just that they spend most of their day lying down eating, so all we ever see is the clumsy version of them. So: less "terrible motor skills" and more "why bother, here's a nice branch and some shade."

Hope that satisfies you! Let me know if you want links to any of it.

Best,
Sam

So when he asks "what do cows drink," it lands on your ears as "what do cows milk," because that is exactly what you have just been saying over and over. Your tongue just repeats the pattern on autopilot and blurted "milk" before your actual knowledge could kick in and correct it. You knew it was water in your head, but your mouth was running on the script he set up with the repetition. Totally normal, happens to literally everyone who tries this. Next time just pause, take a breath, and re-listen to the real question before answering.

Tell your brother he owes you a coffee for that one.

text:
Hey Sam,

Thanks for the email! Great question, and honestly one of my favorite ones to geek out about. I was eating cold mozzarella the other day and thinking the same thing, so I actually did a bit of digging and here's the deal.

When cheese is cold and solid, the fat and the protein are locked together in a tight little matrix, kind of like everyone's shoulders pressed together in a crowded elevator. Your tongue can only really get to the surface of that matrix, so you mostly taste the surface, which is salt and a little sharp bite. All that richness sitting inside is trapped and can't get to you.

When you heat it up, a couple of things happen at once. The fat melts out and starts to flow, so now your tongue is basically coating itself in liquid fat, and fat is the main delivery vehicle for flavor in food. A lot more of it touching your taste buds at once means way more flavor getting across compared to a cold dense block. The proteins also loosen up as they heat, so more of the tangy, nutty, umami stuff that's actually suspended inside the cheese gets released into your mouth instead of sitting sealed up in the solid. So you're tasting not just the surface anymore but the whole thing at once.

Then there's the browning stuff if it gets hot enough. The Maillard reaction kicks in on the surface, toasts it a little, and those browned bits have their own whole set of flavors, roasted and slightly buttery, that cold cheese just doesn't have at all. That's half the reason a grilled cheese or a pizza slice hits different from cold cheese on a cracker, even if it's the exact same cheese.

And don't sleep on the texture side of it either. Warm, stringy, flowing cheese does something different in your mouth than cold and firm, honestly it's more of a satisfaction thing than a pure taste thing. text:
Hi Sam,

Yes, you've probably noticed it: a whole row of archers on a wall, the director yells "shoot!" and they all let loose at the exact same moment, like clockwork. It looks dramatic, but it's not how any archer unit in history ever worked. So why do they do it?

Because of the sound. A single arrow hitting a shield or a target makes a fairly dull little thump, and one archer shooting out there on a field is barely a sound at all. But when forty archers all release in the same instant, you get one big "thwip-clang" that comes through as a single massive percussive hit in the mix. It's basically the arrow equivalent of a gunshot. If they'd been drawn and released over two or three seconds the way real volleys actually went, the audio would just smear out into a small raspberry noise and the whole battle scene would sound pathetic. The director wants one clean hit, so he gets one clean hit, and the only way to engineer that is to have everyone release together on his mark.

There's also the visual side. A simultaneous release looks like one single action, which reads as power and coordination on camera. A spread-out volley reads as a bunch of people separately doing little bow things, which is honestly more accurate but less impressive. Movie battles want to look like one big event, and the mass release sells that.

Real archery volleys, by the way, were staggered on purpose. If everyone shot at once you'd get a wall of arrows all in one little band and open gaps in the next; good commanders wanted the arrows arriving spread over time so the enemy was under continuous pressure. People also just draw at different speeds, so a true simultaneous release takes actual training to pull off and even then is never perfectly synchronized.

So the short answer: it's for the sound effect and the look, not for accuracy. Every battle archery scene you've ever seen is basically one really big whoosh that the sound team then buried under drums and screaming.

Anyway, let me know if you want to go shoot arrows this weekend. Actual ones, at different times, like normal people.

Cheers,
Alex

Hi Sam,

Fun question! Honestly, pandas look clumsy for a couple of real reasons, not because they're just dummies.

First, size vs. shape. They're stocky, short-legged bears, so they don't really flow the way a deer or a cat does. Climbing a bamboo tree is basically a climbing wall for them, and they usually only bother with the young ones when they're small enough to haul to a better spot.

Second, their whole motor system is tuned for eating, not athleticism. That "thumb" they use to hold bamboo? It's just an extended wrist bone, not an actual extra digit. It gives them a grip that works great for stripping stalks but is a fraction as dexterous as a primate's hand. So grabbing, stacking, and fine manipulation all look awful on camera.

Third, most of the clumsy stuff you see is grown-ups playing with cubs, which naturally looks like slapstick. And a lot of the embarrassing clips are from zoo pandas in small enclosures. Wild ones are quietly pretty good at walking around without falling into ditches - they just never do anything impressive enough for YouTube.

So: specialized hands, heavy bodies, and a camera bias. Not actually bad at being a bear.

Best,
Alex

text:
Hey Sam,

Good question, and the two do get tangled up. The short version: satire is the goal, parody is the tool.

Satire is about using humour, exaggeration, or irony to criticise something at large - politics, human nature, a whole industry. The thing being mocked is the point. You do not need to copy any specific work; you are pointing at the world.

Parody is the technique of imitating a particular style, work, or format so closely that it becomes ridiculous - a fake IKEA manual, a spoof of a famous movie scene. The imitation itself is what generates the joke, and it can be aimed at pretty much anything, including just the original work rather than some bigger target.

So they overlap a lot - parody is one of satire's favourite tools - but satire can work without parody, and parody can just be there to be funny without criticising anything.

Let me know if that clears it up.

Cheers,
Alex

text:
Hey Sam,

Good question! It comes down to where the traffic comes from. The Super Bowl stream is basically one file: one or a few big video servers push the same content to everyone. Cable providers have peering deals and content delivery networks (stuff like CDNs) that put copies of that stream on servers right inside their own networks, so the video never really travels across the internet at all. It's local, and since everyone watches at the same time, the provider just reserves a big chunk of capacity for it in advance. A paid, scheduled event they plan for.

A "crazy event" - say a local emergency, a stadium fight, a tweet that goes viral - is the opposite: millions of people in different neighborhoods all uploading and downloading random stuff at once to all over the internet. That's a bunch of different destinations, two-way, and it all has to actually cross the backbone through the ISP's point of presence, which is a fixed-size pipe. Nobody planned for it, there's no CDN copy of "everyone in town filming the same aisle," and it all hits at once. So the pipe fills up and things crawl.

Same internet, totally different traffic shapes.

- Alex

Hi Sam,

Funny you should ask, because I'd put it the opposite way: lifting with the legs is mostly the default, and bending to grab stuff with a rounded back is what we have to fix. Babies climbing onto furniture don't groan and hunch over; they squat, brace, and push off things with their legs. A stiff upright torso with a hip hinge is just how the body moves when it's not trying to coddle its spine.

So no, it's not some deep learned behaviour you have to unlearn. It's a small one, picked up from how we actually grab things day to day: we lean down from the waist because that takes less effort than walking around to the thing, crouching, and squatting under it. Nobody eavesdrops and says "nice lift"; you just grab the bag on the floor and it drags your torso down with it. By age four you've done that a few thousand times and the shortcut is set, and for a shoe on the doorstep the shortcut works fine.

It stops working when the thing is heavy, because now the load is out in front of you and your lower back has to hold your whole upper body plus the weight mostly in compression, which is exactly the loading that herniates discs. Legs and glutes are the body's big motors; the back's job in a lift is to stay stiff, like the grey structure of a crane while the cable does the work.

So it's less unlearning than just learning the other way a few hundred times until it's the first thing you reach for. A gym is basically a place where someone yells at you nicely while you practise the squat version of picking things up.

Anyway, drinks next week still on?

text:
Hi Sam,

Ha, yes, the hot-soup nose. It's a real thing and it actually has a couple of different causes wrapped up in one, so let me try to untangle it.

The main one is about mucus, not tears. Your nose and sinuses are normally kept coated in a thin layer of mucus that's meant to be runny-ish so it can trap dust and bugs and get swept out by cilia. When you do heat that works on the blood vessels in your nose. Hot food and especially hot drinks raise the temperature of the mucosa, the blood vessels in there dilate, and more fluid leaks out of those vessels into the mucus. It goes from thin and clear to a lot more fluid, and it just starts running. Nothing's wrong, it's a blood vessel reaction, kind of like the way your face gets red and sweaty from hot food. That's also why it's more bad with soup and tea than with, say, a hot sandwich.

Then the spice layer, if you're eating anything spicy in there. Capsaicin (the burn in chili) and stuff like black pepper hit the TRP channels in your nasal lining, which are the same heat-and-burn sensors, and that triggers an extra wave of mucus plus the watery-eyes reflex. So a hot spicy noodle soup is basically two triggers stacked, and that's when it's genuinely miserable.

The thing people always get wrong is the steam thing. It's not the steam on the surface running down your nose, it's the heat and the irritants getting into your nose through the normal airway while you're eating. You can get it from a hot drink with no visible steam at all. And it tends to lap off a bit after a few minutes once you stop eating, because the vessels calm down.

So the short version: hot stuff = warm blood vessels in your nose = more fluid in the mucus = it runs. Spice on top = extra run. If it only happens with hot/sharp and not with cold air or dust or allergies, it's harmless and there's nothing to fix, just eat the soup with a straw and a bigger towel. It's only worth bothering a doctor about if it also happens with things that aren't hot or spicy, because that starts to sound like an allergy or an irritation instead.

Anyway, that's my best shot. Tell me if it's actually the spicy one that's making you do it because that part has a different answer.

Cheers,
Alex

Hi Sam,

Good question, and honestly a fair one on the surface. But I think it rests on a premise that's a bit off in both directions.

First, most modern Christians actually treat Jesus far higher than a mere prophet - basically as God incarnate. Jesus in mainstream Christianity isn't a man who delivered a message; he's the message, the creator of the world, the judge of the final day. So the bar you're comparing to is already off the charts.

Second, Muslims don't put Muhammad above that bar. They explicitly reject worship of him or any superhuman powers in him. No praying to him, no asking him for intercession in the core practice (sufi exceptions exist, sure, as in Catholic saint veneration). The things that do get him high reverence - the Quran being preserved as his exact words, the hadith tracked down, the practice of following his example (sunnah) as the working model for the book - actually map pretty closely onto what Christians do with the Gospels and the apostles, just taken more seriously.

So it's less "they worship Muhammad like we worship Jesus" and more "they take recorded human testimony more literally than most modern (post-critical) Christians do with theirs." The gap is less theology than biblical scholarship.

Anyway, happy to keep going on this.

- Alex

text:
Hi Sam,

Funny you should ask, because I've been thinking about this too. It's actually a mix of chemistry and physics, and it all comes down to what happens to cheese's internal structure when it hits heat.

First, the fat. Cold cheese has its fat locked inside little solid globules, mostly invisible to your tongue. When you melt it, that fat turns liquid and coats everything. Fat is basically a flavor-delivery vehicle, and a surprising amount of the stuff that makes cheese taste like cheese is fat-soluble. So once it's warm, way more of that flavor is actually reaching your taste buds instead of being trapped in the cold solid matrix.

Second, the proteins. Cheese is really just a network of casein proteins holding water and fat in place. Heat breaks down parts of that network, so the water and fat are free to move, and things can escape. This leads to the big one, which is volatiles. A huge chunk of what you experience as "taste" is actually smell, and cold cheese holds its aromatic compounds inside pretty tightly. Heat makes them evaporate and drift up into your nose, which is where most of flavor gets processed in your brain. Warm food smells way more than cold food for exactly this reason, and a plate of melted cheese is basically a small volatile buffet going off.

And then there's the texture thing, which tricks your brain into rating the whole experience higher. Melted cheese is warm, stretchy, drapey, and it clings to whatever it's on. That contrast, especially on crispy pizza crust or crisp bread, is genuinely pleasurable. Your brain reads "warm, soft, stretches, clings to a crunch" as delicious even before the actual flavors fully register. It's the same reason warm bread tastes better than cold bread, or why warm soup hits differently than cold soup.

So put it together: more liquid fat carrying flavor around, more smell escaping into your nose, and a warm stretchy texture your brain already likes. Cold cheese is basically the same flavors locked in a box, and melting just gets the box open and turns on the little fan.

Let me know if you want me to explain why cheap shredded cheese melts worse than the good blocks, because that one is a totally different story involving anti-caking dust and pre-stretched proteins.

Talk soon,

text:
Hey Sam,

Great question, I've been mulling it over too. I think it comes down to a few things stacking up in the developer's favor.

First, what the game actually is. Minecraft is basically a sandbox of blocks with a tiny number of rules. Everything in the world is data - just a grid of block IDs - so modding is mostly editing data and adding a few new types of things. Skyrim is the opposite extreme on the surface (huge handcrafted world), but under the hood it uses the Creation kit, which is a full level editor the devs literally released to the public. So Skyrim modders inherit a professional authoring pipeline. When "making content" maps cleanly onto a tool someone gave you, modding takes off.

Second, the tech. Games modded in Lua, or with exposed scripting hooks, or running on engines with readable .xml/.json config files, are moddable. Games where everything is compiled into one opaque binary and the save file is encrypted are basically unmoddable, and most modern AAA games are exactly like that. A lot of it is corporate fear - they worry mods will break saves, crash the multiplayer, or get them sued, so they lock everything down. Single-player games get away with being open.

Third, multiplayer. This is the big one. Any big networked game (Fortnite, Destiny, WoW) essentially cannot have a normal modding scene because a mod on one player's machine changes what everyone sees, and there's no way to verify that a thousand strangers are running compatible code. Someone will exploit it immediately. So you get official cosmetic systems instead, which look modding-ish but aren't.

Fourth, it's a cold-start problem. Modding communities are network effects: the first 100 mods make the next 1000 trivial by showing everyone what's possible and providing libraries. If a game launches with zero modding infrastructure, it rarely gets one later, even if it's technically moddable, because each modder has to rebuild the wheel. Skyrim had BSA archives and a wiki and a mod manager all within a year.

So: open tech, single-player, a released editor or scripting hook, and an early push from the devs = huge mod scene. Compiled binary, multiplayer, encrypted saves = none. Most games fall on the locked side by default, which is why it feels surprising when a game ends up moddable.

Anyway, tell me if you want me to send you that list of moddable engine games I made.

- Alex

text:
Hi Sam,

Good question, and honestly it's less one thing than a few things piling on top of each other. When something tragic or shocking happens, the brain dumps a ton of adrenaline and stress hormones, which narrows attention to right now and shoves the normal sense of time to the back burner. You stop checking the clock, stop expecting the next break to come, so the "bookkeeping" that makes stretches feel long just goes quiet. At the same time your memory encoding gets disturbed, so afterwards the event can feel oddly compressed, as if an hour held a whole day, or a whole day went by in a minute. Add the fact that in crises people are doing continuous, absorbing action with no idle gaps, and gaps are a big part of how we sense elapsed time in the first place. So it's adrenaline narrowing focus plus memory scrambling plus no downtime, all at once. It's why emergency rooms and disasters feel like they run on their own clock.

Anyway, that's my best shot at it. Let me know if you wanted the psychology-paper version and I'll dig one up.

Talk soon
Alex

text:
Hey Sam,

Good question, and it's not actually that different in the two cases.

For the Super Bowl, your cable box gets the show over the cable network, which is a broadcast TV system. The signal goes out to everyone on one channel and your box just tunes into it. Nobody's downloading a file, so a million viewers in your area don't each pull a copy through your neighborhood lines. That's why it doesn't slow down. (If you were streaming it on the internet instead, it absolutely would be affected.)

The crazy events, like a big traffic jam, a sports result, or a funny video blowing up, all make people use the internet at the same time - checking news, posting pictures, streaming video. All of that is shared pipe traffic, and your ISP's last-mile connection to your neighborhood only has so much capacity. When everyone hammers it at once, each person gets a sliver, so everything crawls.

So it's really: broadcast TV = one copy sent to all, internet = everyone downloads their own copy at the same time. Congested pipe vs. shared channel.

Anyway, happy to explain more if you want.

- Alex

text:
Hey Sam,

Good question, and one I get asked a lot. A few things I think clear it up.

First, the premise is a bit off. For Muslims, Muhammad isn't a prophet in the "occasional visionary" sense; he's the final prophet, the one whose message closes and completes the prophetic line, and the one through whom the Quran was delivered literally word-for-word. Christians also believe Jesus spoke with divine authority, but the Bible is understood as divinely inspired, not dictated. That difference alone makes the Prophet's words carry more weight in daily practice.

Second, Muslims have a huge body of hadith and seerah, so his personal conduct became a legal and moral reference point, referenced thousands of times in the primary sources. We don't have anything comparable for Jesus, whose own recorded sayings are limited. So it's not so much worship of the person as the fact that his life is primary source material.

Third, modern Christianity is pretty decentralized and post-denominational, so Jesus is often a spiritual symbol rather than a lawgiver. Muhammad, by contrast, was legislator, judge, and state founder, all in one.

So: more sources, final authority, and he governed a polity. It adds up.

Talk soon,
Alex

text:
Hi Sam,

Funny you should ask, because I was just standing over a piece of toast trying to figure out the exact same thing. The short answer is that heat does a lot of things to cheese all at once, and almost all of them happen to be in your favor.

Cheese is basically a sponge. Cold and fresh, the fat is solid-ish and trapped in a tight protein network, so every bite is a mix of waxy fat and rubbery casein, and most of the flavor compounds are locked inside and never make it to your nose properly. Melt it, and the fat liquefies and that protein network loosens up. That does two big things: it turns the cheese from something you chew into something that coats your entire mouth, and it frees up the flavor molecules. A lot of what we experience as "taste" is actually smell coming up the back of your throat, and melted cheese lets all those volatile flavor compounds escape, so it hits you on every single bite. Cold cheddar is quiet; melted cheddar has a voice.

Then there's the Maillard reaction. The moment the surface gets hot enough, the sugars in the cheese start reacting with amino acids and you get roasted, toasty, almost nutty notes that simply do not exist in the cold cheese at all. That golden crust on the edge of a grilled cheese is pure Maillard, and honestly I think that crust might be doing more for the "wow factor" than the soft melt underneath.

There's also a sneaky physics point: cold food tastes blander partly because cold suppresses how well flavor compounds dissolve and reach your taste receptors. Warm food just reads as more intense, full stop. Same cheese, same ingredients, eighty degrees difference, and the whole thing tastes richer because your mouth is warm too, so the fat spreads out evenly instead of sitting in little waxy lumps.

So it's not one magic trick. It's liquid fat coating your tongue, way more smell getting out, a little browning on the surface, and the general rule that basically everything tastes better warm. Your friend who says melted is "cheese at its peak" is right, and the one who still prefers it cold on a cracker is fighting physics the whole time.

Anyway, save me a piece of toast.

— Alex

text:
Hey Marcus,

Haha, finally you asked me one of the actual physics questions. So G-suits, the ones fighter pilots wear, basically fight the problem of your blood pooling in your legs when you pull hard. When you pull 6 or 7 Gs in a turn, your blood "weighs" six or seven times more than normal, and gravity plus the turn just slams it all down into your lower body. Your brain is at the top of the column, so it doesn't get enough blood, you get gray-out, then you black out, and the pilot loses the plane. Pretty simple and pretty bad.

A G-suit is basically a set of air bladders wrapped around your legs and belly, connected to a pump. It's kind of like a really aggressive pair of compression socks that inflate. As the plane pulls G, sensors in the suit (and sometimes the plane's hydraulics) tell it how much G you're under, and it inflates the bladders to squeeze your legs and lower torso. That pressure pushes the blood back up toward your heart and brain so you don't faint. It also stops your stomach from sliding down, which helps, though that's the lesser problem.

The timing is the tricky part. If it inflates too early or too hard, it traps blood in your legs and actually makes the problem worse once the G lets off, so you get this woozy inverted feeling when you come out of the turn. So the suit has to ramp up with the G and bleed off fast when the G drops. Modern ones use the plane's actual G data to tune it, which is a lot smoother than the old ones where the pilot basically felt themselves going gray and squeezed the lever.

To be fair, the suit is only part of the story. Pilots also do this strain maneuver they're trained in, where they tense up their whole lower body on command and breathe in short sharp bursts to keep blood in their chest. That plus the suit plus some innate tolerance is how guys hold 9 Gs for a few seconds. Without the suit I think the average pilot blacks out around 4 or 5.

Anyway, you could probably guess the follow-up question: no, I would not trade seats.

Talk soon,
Alex

Hi Sam,

Good question - people mix them up a lot. The short version: satire sets out to criticize something (politics, society, human folly) to make a point or prompt change. Parody imitates the style of a particular work or artist for comic effect - it mocks the form, not a cause.

So a satire might be a show lampooning how politicians talk, to make you think about politics. A parody would be a sketch done in the exact mannerisms of one specific comedian, just to get laughs at their style.

The useful test: if it targets an idea or institution to change how people see it, that leans satire. If it copies a specific artist's style for the joke, that's parody. They often overlap, though - a great parody can carry satire inside it.

Hope that clears it up - ping me if you want examples.

Best,
Alex

text:
Hi Sam,

Great question - I've been thinking about this a lot since going down the Skyrim modding hole. I think it mostly comes down to whether the developers actually wanted other people to be able to mess with their game, and a few structural things that follow from that.

The biggest factor is access. If the game exposes its data in a readable way - plain text files, open script languages, tools that come with the game - people can mod it. If everything is compiled, encrypted, or locked inside sealed bundles with zero docs, modding just isn't feasible. Skyrim shipped with the Creation Kit, which is basically a full editor: you can make new quests, spells, perks, literally new worlds, and save them as plugins. Minecraft's data files were basically readable from day one, and Java is a language people already knew. So the barrier to entry was "figure out a text file" instead of "reverse engineer a proprietary binary format."

Second is architecture. Games that are data-driven work better for modding. If a sword is just a row in a spreadsheet saying "damage: 15, weight: 2," adding a new sword is trivial. If the sword's behavior is hardcoded into the engine, you'd need to recompile the game. Skyrim, Elder Scrolls games in general, and most RPGs/CRPGs (Baldur's Gate, Divinity) lean heavily on data tables, which is why they all got mod scenes. A game like a tightly-coded twin-stick shooter or a puzzle game doesn't have that structure at all - there's nothing to plug in.

Third is what modding gives you. Modding communities stick around when mods can do something the base game can't - entirely new quests in Skyrim, new biomes and items in Minecraft. That's creation, not just tweaking a difficulty slider. Games where "the content" is the only thing that matters (open worlds, sandboxes, RPGs) benefit way more than games where the content is twelve handcrafted levels whose whole point is their specific tuning.

And finally, just culture: if the devs don't actively crack down on mods or break them every patch, a community forms and then sustains itself. Bethesda is famously hands-off, which lets mods pile up for a decade. A developer who patches out every third-party hack on day two kills it before it starts.

So short version: open tools and data, data-driven design, content that mods can meaningfully expand, and devs who don't fight it. Miss any one of those and you get an empty "modding" wiki page.

Talk soon,
Alex

Great question. Most of it just washes away: rain and snowmelt dissolve the salt and the water carries it off into gutters, streams and rivers, eventually to the sea. Melting also spreads it deep into the roadbed and soil where it leaches downward. The salt near the road is constantly renewed, but dilution and runoff keep any one patch from accumulating forever.

Still, you're right that it adds up - tracks full of ploughed salt and tugpaths beside roads show salt build-up, and it does kill trees along busyroutes over time, hence salt-tolerant planting now.

Hey Sam,

Great question, and genuinely fun to answer. Short version: they don't, not exactly - 55 gallons is just the standard drum size that the whole industry grew up around, and it stuck.

The drum traces back to oil barrels. In the 1860s, when Pennsylvania was pumping out all that oil, shippers needed a standard container, and the barrel won out. The point of all that history is this: once big industries standardize on one drum size, everything builds around it - the racks, the forklifts, the pallets, the shipping containers all get designed for that single size. In the US the standard steel drum is 55 gallons, and in a lot of other parts of the world it's 200 liters, which is basically the same thing (200 L is about 52.8 US gallons) - the metric system got close and just rounded.

So why is it exactly 55? A few practical things pile up. The standard drum is 33-3/4 inches tall and 23 inches in diameter, which gives roughly 55 gallons. The dimensions seem chosen so that (a) one person can handle a drum, (b) forklifts and pallets move numbers that fit nicely onto a truck or into a shipping container, and (c) the shell material and wall thickness are economical at that size. Nobody picked 55 because it's a nice number; the geometry and the handling requirements picked it, and then everyone agreed to it.

There's a nice little surprise in the paperwork: a "55-gallon" drum doesn't actually hold 55 gallons. It holds about 53-54 to the top rim, and the safe working fill (leaving headspace for expansion and so you can pour without spilling) is usually listed around 51-52. If you've ever filled drums to ship anything flammable, you're following a fill line, not the number on the drum. Same deal with 200 L drums.

So the real answer is: some 19th-century barrel size, plus the constraint that two people plus a forklift and a truck need to be able to move it, plus (don't fill it to the top) = about 55. Standards are just old compromises that got load-bearing.

Anyway, tell me if that's the answer you were after or if you actually need to fill some drums next week - different questions entirely.

Best,
Alex

text:
Hi Sam,

Haha, that's a great question — sitting there trying to hold a bamboo stalk like a spoon and failing spectacularly.

The short answer is that pandas are basically bears wearing a bamboo costume. Their "thumb" they use to grip stalks isn't even a real thumb; it's a flattened wrist bone (the sesamoid) that got repurposed. It works well enough to strip leaves, but it's not a precision tool, so everything looks clumsy from our perspective. On top of that, they're eating low-calorie, low-nutrition grass-like plants, so they only manage a few hours of actual eating a day and spend the rest napping — an underfed, half-asleep animal doesn't have great coordination either. And their vision is pretty poor (they're basically colorblind and nearsighted), which doesn't help with fine motor work.

Evolution-wise, there was no pressure to select for dexterity. They live in dense bamboo forests, don't chase prey, don't make tools, and their main physical challenge is climbing and sloshing through snow — all gross motor skills, which they're actually decent at. So "terrible motor skills" is really "motor skills optimized for a different job than holding a lunch."

Let me know if you want me to send that video of the one trying to open its own food bag again.

— Alex

Hi Sam,

Great question. I think it comes down to the fact that the sceptics were wrong. A fad dissappears, but the Beatles kept writing real songs for fifteen years, and the body of work proved it wasn't a blip: Rubber Soul into Abbey Road is one of the steepest development curves in pop, from chirpy covers to some of the most sophisticated studio work of the 60s. Meanwhile the whole genre they got dismissed in expanded enormously, and everyone who came after - the Stones, Queen, Radiohead, even K-pop - had to answer to them, so they became the reference point. That lock-in matters: you can't unhear what everyone else is built on.

There's also survivorship bias in the "boy band" label. Today's ticky-tacky pop acts vanish in a year, but the Beatles did things that made the journos eat their hats: they quit touring to take control of the studio, they did the rooftop, they sold out Shea Park, half the music press started writing about them as artists precisely because they kept outgrowing the fad. The legend is really just the record of how badly people underestimated them.

Cheers,
Alex

text:
Hi Sam,

Funny you should ask, I was just watching the ref at the park yesterday going mental with his. The little ball you see rattling around in a pea whistle (that's what they're called, apparently) is literally called the pea, and it's the whole secret to the sound.

A normal whistle is just a tube where air hits an edge and makes a steady note - think of that annoying ferry horn thing. But if you put a little ball in there, the moving air catches it and pushes it around the chamber. Every time it bumps the edge, it briefly changes how the air is vibrating, so instead of one clean tone you get this chaotic buzzing shriek. It's basically turning a steady note into a mess on purpose, and a mess is much louder and more attention-grabbing than a clean note would be.

That's why they use them - you need the sound to cut through a crowd or wind, not be pleasant. A whistle without the pea is way quieter and mellow, more like a flute. Some whistles (like the referee ones you see in football) actually have a slotted chamber instead of a free ball, same idea but more consistent, because a pea can get stuck or the sound varies with angle. The old-school pea whistle sounds a bit different every blast depending on which way you're holding it.

So: tiny ball, gets shoved around by air, keeps interrupting the vibration, makes it loud and harsh on purpose. That's it.

Let me know if you want the diagrams, I found some decent ones with the airflow drawn in. Honestly the fact that someone looked at a whistle and thought 'yeah we should put a ball in that' is one of my favourite bits of engineering.

Cheers,
Alex

text:
Hi Sam,

Good question, and the short answer is yes, new tools do partly depend on old ones, but you can still push accuracy forward. A few tricks make it work.

First, combine measurements: if you have several slightly different tools, you can average or cross-check them to squeeze out a better value than any one of them alone.

Second, use a clever indirect method. Often you can measure a new quantity by comparing two things that should be exactly equal, so the errors cancel rather than adding up. Rulers get made this way: you lay many copies of the old ruler end to end and build a longer master, so the old error doesn't grow.

Third, let physics set the standard. Once you have something stable and reproducible to define the unit itself, like a fixed frequency of light for the meter, every new tool can be checked against that rather than against an older tool.

So it's a slow staircase, not a dead end.

Best,
Alex

То есть один и тот же сценарий: реактор остановлен, но тепло выводить нечем.

Вторая — Fehler в конструкции или на управлении, которая приводит к перегреву без остановки. В Чернобыле эксперимент на пониженной мощности вскрыл положительный паровой коэффициент и блокировку защит: при разгерметизации защита затормозила, мощность пошла вверх и расплавила каналы. Это другая причина — не «остыть нечем», а «нагревало сильнее, чем надо».

Так что в большинстве случаев — потеря охлаждения, а отдельно случаи, где система управления дала сбой прямо во время работы.

Привет, Сань!

Спасибо за письмо, вопрос в точку, потому что вариант из того поста — с экспертизой и согласованиями — у многих в тупик уходит, и люди остаются с домом, который по документам «не дом».

Во-первых, есть путь через суд. Приводишь дом в нормальное состояние (коммуникации, утепление, чтобы зимой была нормальная температура) и подаёшь иск о признании права собственности на здание, которое фактически является жилым домом, а не хозяйственным строением на садовом участке. Суд смотрит на фактическое использование и техническое состояние. Шансы нормальные, если дом капитальный, а не щитовой, и ты там реально живёшь всезонно, а не приезжаешь на уик-энды. Минус — нужно заключение специалиста, его назначает суд, и это деньги плюс время на несколько месяцев.

Во-вторых, если дом у тебя на участке, где уже разрешено жилищное строительство, можно просто оформить ввод в эксплуатацию по упрощёнке для самостроя: в администрацию или МФЦ с декларацией и техпланом от кадастрового инженера. Суд не нужен, всё быстрее. Работает именно тогда, когда статус земли это позволяет, посмотри публичную карту.

В-третьих, самый основательный вариант: перевести сам участок из садовых земель в земли ИЖС через изменение ВРИ, через публичные слушания. Медленно, на полгода-год, но потом дом перестает быть «дачным» вообще, и все вопросы закрываются сами.

Так что выбирай по ситуации: дом нормальный по строению, а виноваты бумаги — суд или самострой; дело в статусе земли — меняй ВРИ. Напиши, что у тебя за участок и как дом построен, подскажу точнее.

Давай на связи,

text:
Hey Sam,

Great question, and the answer is that those two cases are actually pretty different.

The Super Bowl doesn't show up on the open internet at all. The game travels over a private, pre-arranged pipe between the broadcast network and the cable/satellite company (or as a reserved deal with a streaming service). The carriers plan for it months ahead, reserve the bandwidth in advance, and it never has to compete with anyone else's traffic. It's like having your own private lane on a highway.

A "crazy event" - a huge game going viral on a regular streaming site, a game server getting hammered, a national event where everyone logs on at once, that sort of thing - all of that rides the shared public internet. Then ISPs hit the limits of their normal capacity, and a lot of them deliberately run traffic management (throttling) during peak congestion to keep everyone from crawling instead of just some people from crawling. So you notice it.

So it's not that millions watching the Super Bowl are magic - it's that those millions are on a private reserved channel, while the crazy-event crowd is all in the same shared lane.

Let me know if that makes sense, I can dig deeper.

- Alex
